newsitem.title: UK: Euro heavy fuel oil's summer surge suprises.
newsitem.headline: Euro heavy fuel oil's summer surge suprises.

text.p: European heavy fuel oil has enjoyed an unseasonal 10 percent surge in value since June, surprising many who had banked on it taking its traditional summer dive, say traders.

Fuel oil barges in the Rotterdam area have gained some 10 percent to trade at over $90 a tonne in a season where weak utility demand and heavy Russian exports were expected to push the benchmark product lower.
Barges are now changing hands at levels not seen since March, the tail-end of the winter buying period.
"Its more buoyant than in past years," said one dealer for a major refiner. "It took a lot of people by surprise and if you'd gone short it was painful."

Heavy U.S. refinery buying in Europe and thinner than anticipated summer exports from Russia were the major causes said some, though others denied that Baltic and Black Sea fuel flows were any less than expected.

With crude refining margins poor in June, U.S. refiners found it more profitable to crack residual fuels and their buying spree dried up high sulphur straight-run fuel markets, normally fed by Russian exports.

Bunker-grade cracked fuel oil also left the region via an arbitrage window that has stayed open unusually long, with cargoes going to Cuba and new markets for Russian fuel oil being opened in Mexico and Panama.
"The arb to the States has been open for a considerable time so Russian fuel has been bypassing the ARA area or even coming out of ARA, lowering stocks there" a trader said.

Local production can not replace barrels shipped out of the region. Start-up of Shell's $1.7 billion "Per+" complex in Rotterdam, which will cut 1.4 million tonnes annually from fuel oil output, is gradually eating into supply.
Opinions are divided on whether fuel oil's strength will continue into the autumn or prove a brief blip.

Better crude margins and a tighter arbitrage to the States may limit straight-run buying, leaving barrels to weigh on the bunker market. But others see trans-atlantic shipments continuing to hold up values in Europe.

Stanislav Gorbunov of Finnish-based Russian fuel exporter Crudex said his company expected to ship 200,000 tonnes of both cracked and straight-run M100 fuel trans-atlantic in August, the same volume as in July.

Gorbunov said river exports from inland refineries, only possible when winter ice melts in the waterways, were not matching estimates because of high inland crude prices and soaring rail and barge transportation costs.
Analysts predicted peak exports from Russia this year at 1.8 million tonnes a month or more.
Geneva-based consultants Petrologistics said export volumes were averaging around 450,000 tonnes a week.
"There has been an increase but not as much as we had anticipated," said Petrologistics' director Conrad Gerber. "The numbers are not startling."
But traders marketing fuel out of St. Petersburg insisted volumes were heavy, with one seeing 1.5 million tonnes moving out of the port in May, June and July.

Overall steady numbers reflected a shift in export traffic from the Black Sea to Baltic ports, from where product can be more easily traded by the few big companies that now control most Russian sales, he said.

Whichever way the price swings now, its rise proved there was still life left in a market that many considered doomed to oblivion by the environmental pressure to shift to less sulphurous fuels, traders said.
